articles.title: Judge wants former U.S. attorney to investigate whether the government misled her in Trump golf case
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — A federal judge said Saturday she intends to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor in the nation’s capital during President Donald Trump’s first term to investigate whether she was purposefully misled by lawyers and administration officials in a lawsuit challenging one of his prized Washington construction projects, the renovation of a historic public golf course along the Potomac River.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — A federal judge said Saturday she intends to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor in the nation’s capital during President Donald Trump’s first term to investigate whether she was purposefully misled by lawyers and administration officials in a lawsuit challenging one of his prized Washington construction projects, the renovation of a historic public golf course along the Potomac River. Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, would examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Department of Justice violated ethics or misled U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes during the course of the case that was initiated in February by the DC Preservation League and two golfers. The Republican administration plans to close the East Potomac Golf Course and park on Nov. 15 with the intention of constructing a “World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events.” An injunction issued by Reyes last month temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the course, and the administration must give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any “irreparable modification” to any “forms or features” of the course while the lawsuit is active. Reyes is giving each side a chance to be heard on her plan to name Liu as special master in the case. They must do so in writing by Friday, when the next court hearing in the dispute is scheduled. Reyes, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden, wants to know whether federal officials lied about the extent of renovation plans during months of hearings. She also wants to know if they were truthful about various steps they took, including cutting hundreds of trees early last month. She announced during a hearing Oct. 30 that she was starting a formal investigation of the government’s conduct. Earlier in the case, she had rejected numerous motions from the plaintiffs to step in, saying she trusted the government attorneys. As the city’s chief federal prosecutor, Liu oversaw some of the matters referred to her office by then-special counsel Robert Mueller during his investigation into possible ties between Trump’s 2016 campaign and Russia. Trump later nominated her to be associate attorney general, the third-highest-ranking Justice Department job. Liu withdrew from consideration after running into opposition on the Republican-led Senate Judiciary Committee because of her past membership in a lawyers’ group that has supported abortion rights. She eventually resigned from the group because, she said previously, it took left-leaning positions, and she is now part of her own law firm, Liu Shur Kravis LLP. David Super, a law professor at the Georgetown University Law Center, said the initiation of a formal investigation by a judge to look into the conduct of a trial’s participants “can be a precursor to holding someone in contempt of court.” Super said it also is a reflection “of the difficulty she had in determining who initiated the tree-cutting in defiance of the assurances DOJ provided. She doesn’t have the time to keep holding long, complex hearings and so wants a special master to narrow the issues.” Reyes ordered the Oct. 30 hearing after multiple Truth Social posts by Trump indicated there were plans for the golf course, and construction was expected to begin Nov. 15. Trump said the park would be closed for 15 months while work goes on. The presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic in multiple court hearings afterward when administration officials could not confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually asked whom she should trust. The Justice Department filed notice Oct. 28 that the plans were real.

articles.title: Sotomayor says she hopes Supreme Court will overturn presidential immunity decision
articles.summary: Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor said on Saturday that she hopes the court’s decision granting former presidents broad criminal immunity will be overturned, saying her colleagues have done some “crazy things.” Appearing for a civics education talk at George Washington’s Mount Vernon estate, the liberal justice also publicly commented for the first time on this…
articles.body:
Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor said on Saturday that she hopes the court’s decision granting former presidents broad criminal immunity will be overturned, saying her colleagues have done some “crazy things.”

Appearing for a civics education talk at George Washington’s Mount Vernon estate, the liberal justice also publicly commented for the first time on this week’s midterm contests, when Democrats swept control of both chambers of Congress.

“We saw the outpouring of voters in on Tuesday,” Sotomayor said, though she made no direct mention of the country’s leftward shift, only the turnout.

“I tell people all the time, there’s no excuse for not voting. There just isn’t. Apathy is not acceptable,” she added.

Those comments were interspersed in the justice’s hourlong appearance as part of a multi-day event at the first president’s estate celebrating the country’s 250th anniversary.

Sotomayor focused most of her remarks on the importance of civics education — she serves on the board of iCivics, the education group founded by the late Justice Sandra Day O’Connor — but at times expressed concerns about the state of democracy. She said it would take “some hard work” for the country to get back on an “even keel.”

“There have been some systemic changes in my court’s jurisprudence in many areas of law,” Sotomayor said. “We’ll settle down, too. Not quite sure when. But we will. And a new order will be established that people will begin to understand.”

The justice specifically singled out the court’s 6-3 decision along ideological lines that former presidents enjoy at least presumptive immunity for their official acts. At the time, the justice wrote that it made President Trump and his successos a “king above the law.”

“I dissent a lot. I’m hoping that the court will take back some of the crazy things that it’s done. I’m only joking — maybe not,” Sotomayor told the crowd on Saturday.

“No, seriously,” she continued. “You know, I’ve spoken openly about this, there’s some opinions that I hope in my lifetime will get overturned. The immunity case is one of them.”

articles.title: There is reason to hope that the Democrats might deliver this time
articles.summary: With a decisive rejection of Trumpism, US voters have given Democrats one more chance — they better not blow it.
articles.body:
In the days since the midterm elections in the United States, many commentators have argued that the “blue tsunami” signalled a popular rejection of US President Donald Trump, but not a new love for Democrats. They are right to warn that if the Democratic Party fails to deliver, it will likely face the same kind of anti-incumbent anger in the next election cycle.

I have personally spilled loads of ink arguing that the Democratic old guard’s embrace of neoliberalism is a huge part of what created the crisis conditions that enabled Trump’s rise to power in the first place, and has severely hampered their ability to stop him over the past decade.

But this election cycle was different in remarkable ways. To put it in plain terms, the Democrats started “sucking less” — not all of them, but a lot of them. And this recent demonstration of “sucking less” is what is presently providing me with at least an ounce of hope that the party might actually manage not to blow this historic opportunity.

How did the Democrats “suck less”? First off, there was a proliferation of progressive economic populist candidates who explicitly took on powerful corporations and positioned themselves clearly as fighters for working-class people. The economic populist insurgency within the Democratic Party gained significant ground in this cycle.

Some might wonder, what took so long? For one, it’s easy to forget that the electoral insurgency within the GOP had an eight-year head start on the insurgency within the Democratic Party — and that head start has been enormously consequential.

In the wake of the 2008 financial meltdown, it was, ironically, conservative anti-establishment energy that first captured populist momentum through the Tea Party. With the help of organisations such as FreedomWorks, that energy was quickly channelled into Republican Party primary contests. By 2014, Tea Party activists had unseated GOP House Speaker Eric Cantor and set the stage for Trump.

Nearly three years after the Tea Party kicked off, Occupy Wall Street was the left’s opening salvo in the populist era. By framing a popular class conflict (the 99% vs the 1%) and naming popular villains (Wall Street and big banks), Occupy dramatically changed the national “common sense” about the evils of runaway inequality.

But the grassroots movement was allergic to the electoral realm. Senator Bernie Sanders’ 2016 presidential run brought Occupy’s core message onto electoral terrain, but it wasn’t until the 2018 midterms — with the election of Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (AOC) and “the Squad” — that the left’s capacity for electoral insurgency caught up with where the right already was in 2009.

Since then, independent progressive organisations such as Justice Democrats, the Working Families Party, Democratic Socialists of America, the Sunrise Movement, and countless local and statewide organisations (for example, PA Stands Up and PA United in my home state of Pennsylvania) have been developing their capacity for recruiting and supporting working-class champions to run for office.

This has been a profound development. Over the course of a decade now, in fits and starts, this groundswell of independent grassroots organising has broken the Democratic Party establishment’s virtual monopoly on candidate recruitment. The 2026 midterms demonstrated a significant increase in capacity to run working-class champions for Congress.

And without diminishing the importance of this long-term organisational investment, it is clear that 2026 also saw an organic proliferation of candidates who ran as champions of the working class. This organic proliferation didn’t happen by chance: It was the result of a profound shift in common-sense notions of what constitutes a winning message.

Over the past decade, a growing chorus of voices in Congress and on the campaign trail has taken up the message Bernie originally popularised, arguing for the same reforms and overhauls, from passing Medicare for All and making housing and childcare affordable, to reining in artificial intelligence (AI) and taxing the rich.

But it took a confluence of events to finally start to break into the mainstream of the Democratic Party in the 2026 cycle.

One key event, unfortunately, was Trump winning a second term. An important casualty of Trump’s second victory was the median Democratic voter’s faith in party leadership. The arc of results and consequences from 2016 to 2024 suddenly cleared the fog, exposing a damning narrative about the party leadership’s negligent qualifications when it came to winning elections.

All that stuff they told us about Bernie being “too far left”, all their wisdom about “electability” was nonsense. The acceleration of the party’s already severe bleed of working-class voters in 2024 and its alarming spread to Black and Latino voters exposed the utter bankruptcy of Democratic leader Chuck Schumer’s lauded affluent suburban swing voter strategy.

The next key event was more uplifting, thankfully. In 2025, in a moment when progressive hopes were at their lowest ebb, suddenly Democratic Socialist Zohran Mamdani showed up out of nowhere with one of the most captivating and inspiring mayoral campaigns in US history, winning the Democratic nomination for mayor of New York City, and then the election.

Mamdani’s incredible message discipline centred around one word: affordability. With a discredited party leadership, mostly missing in action, Mamdani effectively filled a leadership and vision vacuum. Meanwhile, Bernie and AOC were crisscrossing the country, filling stadiums and energising the base with their “Fighting Oligarchy” tour.

On the eve of the 2026 midterm season, economic populism had become the only thing on offer, the only thing that seemed to credibly have a chance. Suddenly, a whole lot of Democratic candidates and officeholders were talking about affordability and the working class.

One of the few things party leadership did right in 2026 was not derailing this growing populist message and momentum. So while Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries remain unpopular, a movement among the rank-and-file and a new crop of economic populist candidates managed to land a coherent and compelling narrative.

An orthodox Marxist might argue that the explanation for the Democratic Party’s failure over the past decade to connect to working-class voters is straightforward: It doesn’t want to bite the hand that feeds it, in other words, billionaires and powerful corporations that provide millions in campaign contributions.

While big money undoubtedly provides significant incentives, I take a perspective more like sociologist Max Weber’s, where the political class has an important degree of “relative autonomy”. Most political operatives genuinely want to win elections, but their ideas about how to do so are constrained and distorted by the elite cultural milieu in which they are embedded.

It’s taken a full 10 years since Trump’s first victory for economic populism to finally break into the elite bubble of the liberal consultant class, or at least to bypass it and finally approach a critical mass of candidates and officeholders in the Democratic Party who grasp how the world has changed, what hardship and precarity most Americans are experiencing, and how to win working-class voters back.

In his 2016 run for president, Bernie was not “ahead of his time”. He was reading the times perfectly. What he was ahead of was an out-of-touch Democratic Party establishment, whose misreading of the times enabled a dangerous authoritarian pseudo-populist to ascend to power and set America’s downward spiralling course for a decade now.

Tuesday’s historic “blue tsunami” was not only the result of Trump’s failures. The 2026 midterm election cycle also saw the start of the remaking of the Democratic Party to be a party that — as Bernie steadfastly exhorts us — fights for the working class.

Yes, sure, Bernie probably would have won the general election back in 2016 and 2020. But more to the point today: Bernie is winning. That is to say, by finally moving towards an economic populist agenda and a commitment to America’s working class, the Democratic Party might just be starting to find its popular voice.

Tuesday’s results do not mean US voters have sworn loyalty to the Democratic Party. But they have given it another chance. A chance to deliver and improve people’s lives. It would be wise and electorally prudent to deliver… bigly.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: New Jersey town reveals staggering $26M theft days after election, sparking backlash
articles.summary: Cranbury Township residents demand answers after a $26 million fraudulent wire transfer was kept secret until days after Election Day in New Jersey.
articles.body: A New Jersey township is facing backlash after officials revealed that $26 million was stolen in a fraudulent wire transfer, with residents questioning why the massive theft wasn't disclosed until more than five weeks later — just days after Election Day. Cranbury Township Mayor Lisa Knierim announced Friday that the municipality had been the victim of a "sophisticated financial theft" involving approximately $26 million. Knierim, a Democrat, said the fraudulent wire transfer took place on Sept. 28, with the funds originally designated for purchasing property to meet the township's affordable housing obligations. A task force involving local, county, state and federal law enforcement agencies, led by the township's police department and the Middlesex County Prosecutor's Office, is working to recover the funds, according to the mayor's statement. CYBERCRIME LOSSES NEAR $21B: 5 WAYS TO PROTECT YOUR MONEY So far, investigators have frozen nearly $17.3 million in assets, leaving approximately $8.7 million outside the reported freeze. The township said the investigation remains active, adding that additional details cannot be released. Knierim's announcement came Nov. 6, three days after the midterm elections and more than five weeks after the theft. Several residents responded to the announcement on the township's Facebook page, questioning the timing of the disclosure and demanding greater transparency from local officials. NEW JERSEY MAYOR WHO CHARGED AT RESIDENT DURING COUNCIL MEETING CONCEDES ELECTION LOSS "I'm interested in knowing why this information was kept under wraps until after Election Day," one commenter wrote. Another asked, "If this occurred on September 28th why is it just now being shared?" The announcement followed Tuesday's local election, in which Democrat Thomas Szczur Jr. defeated Republican Carol Haring with 63.69% of the vote to Haring's 36.32%, according to election results published by the New Jersey secretary of state's office. Szczur's victory preserved Democrats' control of all five seats on the Cranbury Township Committee. The mayor acknowledged residents' concerns in her statement. "We recognize that news of this magnitude will understandably raise questions and concerns among our residents," Knierim wrote. "Those concerns are legitimate, and we take them seriously." NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS Knierim also said the township was taking steps to strengthen financial oversight and maintain municipal operations, noting that the Township Committee plans to introduce ordinances Monday to establish two new positions: assistant township administrator and assistant chief financial officer. The committee also plans to consider hiring a municipal accounting firm for additional financial consulting support, while officials work with insurance carriers to explore potential recovery options. It remains unclear why the township waited more than five weeks to publicly disclose the theft. articles.title: Democrats’ congressional win could strengthen Ukraine’s hand against Russia
articles.summary: Ukraine hopes for more US support but faces uncertainty over Trump’s peace efforts and continued military aid.
articles.body:
Kyiv, Ukraine – Kyrylo, a wounded drone technician from eastern Ukraine, does not care much about the results of midterm elections in the United States.

Tuesday’s vote brought on a “blue wave” of victories for the Democratic Party, which will control both houses in the new Congress and provide a check on President Donald Trump.

But it means little to the Ukrainian servicemen.

“We already learned how not to depend on America,” said the 37-year-old, who is recovering from a heavy contusion in a Kyiv hospital after a Russian glide bomb hit his bunker.

He asked Al Jazeera to withhold his last name in accordance with wartime protocol.

“Trump has let us down so many times, sold us to Russia and we’re still standing and kicking Russian [butt],” he said. “We no longer depend on American money and weaponry. The whole world wants to buy our drones now.”

Under Trump, Washington gradually stopped footing much of Ukraine’s wartime bills. While the amount of financial and military aid nearly reached $200bn from Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion to late 2024, since 2025, the US assistance has slowed to a trickle.

From October 2025 to March, Kyiv received a mere $8.2bn in military aid as part of “legacy pipelines” dating back to US President Joe Biden’s administration. The deals will have cost another $13bn when the supplies are over.

Even though Europe took over most of the financial weight, coughing up $83bn in 2025 alone, almost a third of all weaponry comes from US companies, according to the Kiel Institute, a German think tank.

Some aid may be restored, and the Democrats have pledged to scrutinise Trump’s ties to Russia and conduct sweeping investigations focused on alleged corruption within the Trump family.

The investigations will include their ties to Russian politicians, intelligence and oligarchs, such as Umar Kremlev, who reportedly paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for Donald Trump Jr’s wedding celebrations in the Bahamas in May.

The Democrats have already signalled their readiness to issue subpoenas and force the disclosure of executive branch records, including the ones related to Ukraine, once they take control of Congress on January 3.

“Ukraine’s positions may become stronger,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “But we need to keep bipartisan support.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of the midterm results, “We have bipartisan support.” He said he was “thankful to the Republicans, but Democrats very clearly state their support of Ukraine and providing aid to it.”

But getting more backing from the US Congress is not going to be easy as several Republicans who supported Ukraine have lost their seats.

The “blue wave” unseated Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, who cochaired the Congressional Ukraine Caucus and was one of Kyiv’s staunchest supporters.

Other notable pro-Ukrainian Republicans are Don Bacon of Nebraska, a self-described “Reaganite” staunchly opposed to Russia, and Mike Lawler of New York, who voted for the Ukraine Support Act.

At the same time, Kyiv needs to appoint a new ambassador to Washington. Olha Stefanishyna, a former deputy prime minister, was fired in August during a probe into her “illegal enrichment”.

The ambassador works with Congress and organises contacts with Kyiv and trips by lawmakers to Ukraine.

“That’s why first of all a new ambassador has to be appointed,” Fesenko said.

And while some supporters of the Democrats urge their party to impeach Trump, Kyiv would be on the losing side, analysts said.

“God forbid if Ukraine becomes the focus of a [third] impeachment because of the negative experience during Trump’s first presidency,” Fesenko said. “It made Trump form a stable negative attitude towards Ukraine.”

Trump’s first impeachment in 2019 concerned accusations that he pressured Kyiv to investigate Biden and Biden’s son Hunter, who had been on the board of Burisma, a Ukrainian natural gas company implicated in corruption schemes.

The Democrats said Trump froze $390m in military aid to Ukraine as leverage at a time when Kyiv badly needed US arms to continue fighting Russia-backed separatists.

Now, before the new Congress takes office, Trump is likely to pressure Ukraine to accept a fast-tracked peace deal with Russia.

“Because when Russia isn’t willing to concede, the fastest way to solve the matter – either through a truce or through freezing the war – is only possible if [Trump] twists Kyiv’s arms,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.

“That’s why the next two months will be rather complicated for Ukraine,” he said.

Because Trump at the moment has Republican majorities in both houses, he will “try to show the effectiveness of his policies to decrease the possible level of confrontation with the new Congress”, Tyshkevych said.

The new Congress will have to deal with a dilemma rooted in allegations of corruption involving top Ukrainian officials and their purported embezzlement of US aid.

“On the one hand, there’s a political conviction to keep supporting Ukraine and on the other hand the political necessity to put an end to questions, suspicions and accusations of Ukrainian leaders in corruption,” he said.

Pro-Kremlin voices are already counting Moscow’s possible losses.

“The Democrats will double down on their efforts to prevent Trump from establishing a dialogue with Moscow, demand the resumption of direct US military aid to Kyiv, insist on the restoration of transatlantic unity on the Ukrainian issue and propose new sanctions against Russia and its main trading partners,” Moscow-based political analyst Andrey Kortunov wrote in an opinion piece for the Kommersant daily.

The Democrats “will initiate investigations into how he negotiates with us”, Moscow-based analyst Malek Dudakov told the Gazeta.ru daily.

The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs dismissed the concerns, saying Moscow’s foreign policies “don’t depend on the fluctuations of the political barometer in other nations”.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, meanwhile, spoke in flattering terms, saying, “President Trump continues to exercise his powers. We sincerely hope that he will continue his peacemaking efforts.”

articles.title: Inside a rancher family's clash with gov't that could have ripple effect right to SCOTUS: ‘Existential threat’
articles.summary: Wade and Teresa King say Washington's Department of Ecology fined them $267,540 over stockwater ponds the state claims are regulated wetlands.
articles.body: The owners of a multigenerational cattle ranch say they are facing an "existential threat" after the Washington state Department of Ecology fined them hundreds of thousands of dollars over their stockwater ponds, and they are warning the case could have substantial implications nationwide. The department fined Wade and Teresa King, owners of King Ranch in Grant and Douglas counties, $267,540 in 2023 for allegedly damaging regulated wetlands by digging ponds to provide water for their ranching operations. The Kings argue the areas, which they were ordered to restore, are long-standing stockwater ponds for their livestock, not regulated wetlands. The Kings, who have been trying to get their case in front of a jury, told Fox News Digital that, not only is their financial stability at stake, so are the rights of other ranchers. "Losing this fight would be an existential threat," Wade said. "I don't know how we would recover from that, to be honest with you." HOW A LOBSTERMAN'S PRIVACY FIGHT REACHED SCOTUS — AND COULD RIPPLE FAR BEYOND THE WATER: 'AIN'T OVER YET' When the Kings were first hit with the fines and restoration orders, they immediately set out to challenge them. However, the department's required process directed them to bring their case before the Pollution Control Hearings Board (PCHB), an administrative panel that does not provide jury trials. In March, the Kings filed a separate lawsuit in Grant County Superior Court, arguing the case should not be decided by the PCHB and that doing so would violate their right to a jury trial. Months later, a judge dismissed the lawsuit, ruling the Kings first had to complete the administrative process. The Kings appealed the decision, and a Washington Court of Appeals commissioner paused the PCHB proceedings in September while the court considers whether they are entitled to a jury trial. "It's all under the executive branch, and they very rarely go with the property owner," Wade said, adding that Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, who was attorney general when the fight began, now has appointment authority over the board alongside the state Senate. "They almost always side with the agencies and it's just not a fair trial for appellants like us." The PCHB declined to comment due to the pending case. Oliver Dunford, a senior attorney at Pacific Legal Foundation representing the Kings, told Fox News Digital they are prepared to petition the U.S. Supreme Court if they are unsuccessful in Washington. HOW A SIX PACK OF BEER AND THE MAGNA CARTA COULD FINALLY FIX A PROBLEM PLAGUING AMERICANS FOR DECADES "We have to ask them one question: to rule that the Seventh Amendment does apply against the states, and then to argue that the Kings should have had a jury trial under the Seventh Amendment," Dunford said. He said if the case reaches the Supreme Court, a ruling could have ripple effects across other states. "If we prevail, it would have an enormous effect, certainly across the state of Washington, but hopefully across the country, and prevent these agencies from just issuing these fines and then essentially putting the burden on you to prove your innocence and take the case all the way to the Supreme Court just to get a chance at a jury trial," he said. The Kings' attorneys estimate the cost of complying with the department's orders could exceed $3.7 million. But beyond the financial toll, Teresa said the orders would be "unachievable" because the areas were never wetlands in the first place. BLUE STATE'S WATER FAILURES COULD THREATEN FOOD SUPPLIES ACROSS US, LAWMAKER WARNS "How do we as ranchers turn these into wetlands and comply with everything that Ecology wants us to?" she said. "It'll be unachievable and it would just spin us in the ground financially." "How are we supposed to make wetlands from non-wetlands?" Wade added. Wade said the department has failed to give them any details on how to fix the alleged damage. He said the wetlands designation gives the department greater authority over the areas than it would if they were considered stockwater ponds. "That's the big reason why they want to call them wetlands when they're not wetlands," Wade said. Wade and Teresa described how the fight could also hurt their children and their children’s children. The Kings have ranched in Grant and Douglas counties since the 1950s, where Teresa said multiple generations now live and work. TRUMP ADMIN SCRAPS ‘WEAPONIZED’ WILDLIFE RULE THAT BECAME 'BURDEN' ON AMERICAN FAMILIES AND BUSINESSES: BURGUM "It’s fourth generation, then we have fifth and sixth living and working on this ranch, and we want to continue with this," she said. "We just want to be left alone." The department said its investigation found no evidence the areas were previously stockwater ponds and accused the Kings of "damaging 23 naturally occurring wetlands" in Grant County. "Ecology inspectors made site visits to these damaged areas where possible, but also used satellite imagery, aerial images dating from as far back as 1949, and other records to determine that the Kings had damaged 6.37 acres of naturally occurring wetlands by excavating, recontouring, and putting fill in them," the department said. The department added it "repeatedly sought to resolve concerns about the damage" but the Kings "refused to cooperate with these efforts." They said they ordered the Kings to restore 11 more areas in Douglas County last year, bringing the total to 34, and most were on state land. Wade said they have always protected and cared for the land that the department is now accusing them of damaging. "We want clean water," Wade said. "Why would we pollute or cause damage to the land or the water that we rely on in our livelihood? We're generational. Why would we do something to harm ourselves that way and harm the environment?" The Kings said the fight is far from over, with Teresa arguing the case could jeopardize exemptions other ranchers rely on to provide water for livestock. articles.title: Midterm results deliver ‘youth quake’ to American politics
articles.summary: The 2026 midterm elections delivered a solid blue wave for Democrats along with a new class of noticeably younger candidates across the board, beating out both new and incumbent senior opponents. Whether it was James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa in Texas, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Annie Andrews in South Carolina, Melat Kiros in Colorado or Josh Turek in…

The 2026 midterm elections delivered a solid blue wave for Democrats along with a new class of noticeably younger candidates across the board, beating out both new and incumbent senior opponents.

Whether it was James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa in Texas, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Annie Andrews in South Carolina, Melat Kiros in Colorado or Josh Turek in Iowa, young candidates across the country — especially Democrats — defeated older and more experienced opponents in their respective races.

At 29 years old, Kiros is also the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress. Republican Michael Alfonso, 27, beat Democrat Fred Clark, 67, to represent Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District.

Some might call this a “youth wave,” but Santiago Mayer, executive director of the youth-centered pro-democracy group Voters Of Tomorrow, referred to the movement as more of a “youth quake” in scope.

“I think we have seen a lot of energy behind young candidates who understand young people’s frustration with the system and how the system is rigged, not just for older generations, but specifically for rich people in those older generations,” Mayer told The Hill. “We’ve seen Boomers have their net worth increase by almost 30 percent since 2022, whereas for people under 30, it shrunk by 20 percent. We need candidates who are working to fix that.”

Per the Future Caucus’s count , more than 40 non-incumbent millennials won their congressional races in the midterms and 50 others held on to their seats in their reelection bids.

Layla Zaidane, president and CEO of Future Caucus, emphasized that these election results are not a fluke.

“It’s important to remember that waves — especially tsunamis — don’t come out of nowhere,” Zaidane said. “More than a third of congressional candidates this cycle were under 45, up from 1 in 4 in 2024. At least 97 of them — 38 percent of the 272 who ran — have won their races, and Gen Z representation in the House tripled.”

And there are still young candidates out there who could beat their older rivals when the chips fall. In Mississippi, 43-year-old Democrat Scott Colom held a small lead over incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R), 67, as of Friday evening. And in Alaska, Democratic 37-year-old Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins was far outpacing all other candidates in the state’s gubernatorial race.

Zaidane opined that voter priorities this election cycle aligned with what younger candidates are often running on: change.

“This year, voters across the board were looking for exactly that. This crop of candidates also grew up online, so they have strong instincts for communicating consistently and engagingly on the platforms where more people than ever get their news. And they rejected the idea of waiting their turn,” said Zaidane.

And Mayer observed that while younger voters are often treated as single-issue constituents, successful Democratic candidates focused heavily on the economy and the lack of opportunity, going farther than just sympathizing but coming forward with fixes.

The refusal to wait for their turn or apologize for their youth was clear on the campaign trail.

Kiros told NPR back in February, “We need to have leaders that are going to be fighting for the kind of bold policies that actually get something done, and they’re refusing to settle or wait for our turn or ask for permission.”

This strong performance among young newcomers comes as Congress’s advancing age comes under the microscope . Six lawmakers have died during the 119th Congress, most of whom were past the usual age of retirement.

In South Carolina, Sen. Darline Graham (R), 62, was appointed to office after her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), died of an aortic dissection. Despite an endorsement from President Trump and her familial legacy, Graham lost to Andrews, 46.

Trump is the oldest person to be sworn in as U.S. president, and Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) prolonged absence from the Senate this summer for health reasons reignited questions over enacting term limits on lawmakers.

According to Mayer, the midterm results are not simply a rejection of senior lawmakers, but a welcoming in of “new energy” and “new vision” that just happened to be strongly correlated with younger candidates.

“I think obviously there is a lot of exhaustion and exasperation with the system being dysfunctional for young people. I also do think that obviously this being preceded by the 2024 election and what we saw there with regards to the age of the candidates really created an opening for younger people to run and not necessarily on age,” Mayer said.

While his organization’s mission is to build youth political power, Mayer rejects calls for pushing out senior lawmakers, saying he believes governments work best with a mix of young and old.

“I don’t think I would say it’s the end of the gerontocracy because I think we need to have older people who know how things work and have been doing them for a while in there. But I do think it is the end of dominance by older people because the world has simply kind of changed too much,” added Mayer.

While this election heavily favored young, Democratic candidates, both Mayer and Zaidane noted that Gen Z voters have not yet coalesced around one party over the other.

“Gen Z is still forming their political identity, and their support depends on results,” said Zaidane. “Just two years ago, young voters swung right; over the next two years, they’ll judge leaders on housing, jobs, and the cost of building a life, not slogans. Winning their votes is not the same as earning their trust.”

articles.title: From 'Red Sprouts' to school board races, DSA's years-long effort to reach children gains momentum
articles.summary: The DSA's "Socialist Sprouts" curriculum and "Red Sprouts" training aim to bring resistance-driven childcare and radical storytelling to young children.
articles.body: The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is taking its message into classrooms, childcare programs and school boards, urging organizers to approach childcare "from a socialist perspective" through initiatives such as Socialist Sprouts, and it's been an initiative for years, a parental-rights watchdog warns. In New York City, the DSA's "Red Sprouts" program held a training session in October 2026 to equip organizers to provide "resistance-driven childcare" at demonstrations, meetings and community events. The training encouraged participants to incorporate political themes into childcare through "radical storytelling," "cooperative games" and age-appropriate discussions. "There's been a real influx in enthusiasm and their ability and desire to recruit and grow their movement," American Parents Coalition leader Alleigh Marré told Fox News Digital. "What's particularly concerning and insidious, is their direct efforts to apply that to not just adults, but to youth." Marré said the American Parents Coalition is working to equip parents with resources to identify and question political activism in schools, including through its "Lookout" initiative. PARENTS SHOULDN’T NEED THE HELP OF CONGRESS TO SEE THEIR CHILDREN’S SCHOOL CURRICULUM The New York City DSA chapter also established Comrades With Kids, a family-focused organizing group that seeks to be a "political and social home base for working-class families." The group posted photos of DSA-themed coloring pages for children provided at a Zohran for Parents event in September 2025. The New York initiatives are part of a larger effort by the DSA to incorporate childcare and political education into its organizing activities. For years, the DSA's National Political Education Committee has offered training on approaching childcare for activists "from a socialist perspective," including activities for children at organizing events. In 2025, the committee outlined plans to develop a "Socialist Sprouts" curriculum geared for children, parents and caregivers involved in the movement. The organization's efforts to introduce socialist ideas to children date back at least a decade. In 2016, New York City DSA members launched a Socialist Sunday School for children ages 2 to 6. The program used political songs such as "Union Maid" and "Solidarity Forever," alongside children's books, including "The Lorax," to introduce discussions about corporate greed, environmentalism and organizing against unfairness. In Ohio, the Cleveland DSA chapter created a children's coloring book to "help kids learn what we work on at DSA." Its illustrations include a version of "The Three Little Pigs" tied to the chapter's housing agenda. POLITICAL ACTIVISM, ANTISEMITISM ALLEGATIONS PUT PUBLIC SCHOOLS UNDER THE MICROSCOPE The DSA's online store has also sold children's clothing promoting a "Green New Deal for Public Schools." The DSA describes much of its childcare programming as a way to make political organizing more accessible to working-class families. Marré, however, argued that introducing socialist ideas to young children raises concerns about political indoctrination. "The DSA really understands and values that if you can indoctrinate and teach these kids really young, their perceived value of, of socialism, that that's going to stick with kids for a lifetime," Marre said. "It's much easier to teach a child an idea or ideal in their infancy, and when they're very young and they're forming their worldview, and we have seen many efforts to try and capitalize on that." "There's this really concerted effort to instill an ideology in really, really young children, rather than teaching kids how to think and introducing a breadth of ideologies of religious interests, etc.," Marré said. "It's really focused on socialist and communist aligned ideas." Beyond its childcare programs, the DSA has also pursued a strategy to expand its influence over public education through local school board elections. At its 2023 national convention, the DSA adopted an amendment prioritizing the recruitment and support of socialist school board candidates. Rose DuBois, one of the amendment's authors, argued that school board elections could help the organization reach "new kinds of voters, such as parents," while building the infrastructure needed to win higher-profile races. MAMDANI-BACKED SOCIALIST WINS NYC HOUSE SEAT AS DSA EXPANDS ITS REACH IN CONGRESS The Los Angeles chapter of the DSA established its own Public Education Committee, with priorities that include expanding the organization's influence on school boards, recruiting school board candidates, working with teachers unions and promoting policies such as the Green New Deal. Those long-standing efforts come as the DSA gains political ground following the 2026 midterm elections, with DSA-backed candidates winning congressional, state legislative and local school board races. DSA-backed positions prevailed on 23 ballot measures, including a measure in Washington where voters rejected a proposal to restore expanded parental rights in public schools. The election results highlight the growing political reach of an organization whose members advocate shifting economic power away from private corporations and expanding government-funded programs, including universal healthcare and childcare. The 2025 victory of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a card-carrying member of the DSA, heightened awareness of the movement's growing influence, particularly among young people. Following the 2026 midterms, three card-carrying DSA members — Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Reps.-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, both New York Democrats — are set to represent parts of New York City in Congress. Marré said the American Parents Coalition is working to equip parents with resources to identify and question political activism in schools, including through its "Lookout" initiative. She warned that the impact could become more visible as newly elected DSA-backed officials take office. articles.title: 'Trump has cost us': After midterm losses, MAGA asks if it's over

articles.body:
By Ned Parker, John Shiffman, Mike Spector, Peter Eisler and Linda So

DALLAS, Nov 8 (Reuters) - As Republicans faced a nationwide drubbing in Tuesday's midterm elections, supporters streamed out of a Dallas ballroom where they'd hoped to toast a win for US Senate candidate Ken Paxton, a favorite of President Donald Trump.

In the hotel bar, Michael Little, a 59-year-old businessman and three-time Trump voter, stared at the president's image on a television screen. "People are pissed off at Trump. Trump has cost us," he said, capturing a sentiment rippling through the president's Make America Great Again movement after the Republican Party's worst electoral defeat in decades.

Across the coalition, some supporters who once viewed Trump as MAGA's greatest asset are beginning to question whether he's become its biggest liability.

Still, the midterm losses amounted to more than a repudiation of Trump. They ‌were a referendum on the political and cultural movement he built. A defining force in American politics that began as a campaign slogan during Trump's 2016 presidential run now faces a potentially existential reckoning after voters disillusioned with soaring fuel prices, the Iran war and Washington corruption delivered Democrats decisive congressional majorities.

Trump's first major response to the midterms came on Friday. Instead of changing course, he doubled down on the movement's core. He promoted ‌Stephen Miller, the main architect of the administration's hardline immigration crackdown, to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Wiles was seen as a stabilizing force inside an often chaotic White House.

The move was celebrated by some of MAGA's most ardent influencers, who saw it as a return to the anti-immigration agenda at the movement's roots. "Exactly the energy we need," right-wing influencer Benny Johnson posted on X to his 4.1 million followers. "Solid move. It's Miller Time."

The White House did not directly answer Reuters' questions about why Republicans lost, the defeat of candidates who embraced Trump's false 2020 election claims, or where MAGA goes from ​here. Instead, it pointed to Trump's remarks on Wednesday, when he said, "If I were on the ballot, we would have won." He also said it was "largely true" that the Iran war had cost Republicans because "it drove the gasoline up," but that he'd do it again.

For nearly a decade, MAGA has reshaped the Republican Party and transformed national debates on issues such as trade, immigration, race and gender. The movement installed loyalists throughout federal agencies, cracked down on immigration and pressured corporations and public institutions to retreat from diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives. MAGA survived the fallout from the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol and propelled Trump back to the White House. Now, the Democrats' sweeping victory has forced the movement to grapple with an unexpected question: Is MAGA over?

Reuters interviews with more than a dozen MAGA activists, influencers, party strategists, Christian nationalist leaders and researchers who track right-wing politics, along with a review of MAGA supporters' posts and podcasts since Tuesday, show a movement turning its anger on itself.

The stolen-election claims that have driven MAGA since Democrat Joe Biden beat Trump in the 2020 presidential election have mostly gone quiet. Instead, supporters are blaming Republican leaders and Trump's advisers, and in some cases the president himself, for broken promises on living costs, the Iran war and the government's decision to redact or withhold major portions of its investigative files on late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

MAGA's factions also disagree about what comes next. Some want a return to populist and nationalist basics. Some want a movement less tied to one man. And a vocal minority say MAGA is ‌already dead.

"We have to rebuild," Steve Bannon, a prominent MAGA proponent, podcaster and former Trump White House adviser, told Reuters. He urged the party to double down on an ⁠aggressive populist and nationalist agenda and praised Trump for elevating Miller. "Miller's appointment as chief of staff underpins my point," he said. "There is no more hardcore MAGA proponent than Stephen."

As pro-Trump internet forums digested the election results, a notable slice of self-described MAGA loyalists – more than 20% – raised doubts about the movement's leadership and direction, according to an analysis of social media traffic done for Reuters by PeakMetrics, a data intelligence firm. About half of that cohort remained supportive of the MAGA movement but no longer backed Trump as its leader. The other half remained loyal to, though critical of, the president himself.

The analysis was based on 12,850 posts sampled from a universe of 4.6 million Trump-related comments on X and Reddit from 9 p.m. on Election Day to 8 p.m. ⁠the next evening. It found broad concern among MAGA supporters as the results became clear. Of the posts that assigned blame for the rout, nearly a third said concerns about the Iran war and Israel's influence over US policy had overshadowed Trump's message. A quarter said Republicans not fully committed to the MAGA agenda had undermined the movement.

The results left Trump facing large Democratic majorities in both chambers of Congress. In the Senate, Democrats could control as many as 56 of the chamber's 100 seats, more than enough to block Trump's future judicial picks. Republicans might not be able to recapture the Senate until 2032, Republican Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said the morning after the election.

"It's the political equivalent of a meteor strike that went all around the United States," DeSantis said at a post-election briefing.

Democrats will now control governorships in seven battleground states Trump won in 2024 and, strikingly, they won every statewide race in Texas, which hasn't backed a Democratic presidential candidate since 1976.

Since Tuesday, talk of election fraud has virtually vanished among right-wing influencers.

"I have been banging the drum of rigged and stolen elections since ​2020, but ​that is not why we lost the midterms," Rogan O'Handley, a MAGA influencer who posts under the name DC_Draino, wrote on X to his 2.3 million followers. "We lost because we failed to fix the things voters sent us to do." He didn't respond to a request for ​comment.

After the 2020 election, Trump supporter Isabella DeLuca was among thousands who stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021. She was charged with five crimes, including theft of a table from ‌inside the Capitol, and pleaded not guilty. Her case was dismissed after Trump returned to office and pardoned her.

This time, the 26-year-old conservative influencer directed her anger toward what she described as out-of-touch Republican leaders who failed to appeal to Gen Z voters on affordability, avoiding foreign wars and other key issues.

"Republicans were just lazy. They felt like that they were entitled to people's votes and that people would vote for them no matter what," DeLuca told Reuters. "It goes to show you that you do have to earn people's votes, and that even in a super red state like Texas, you're not untouchable."

The MAGA movement this year appeared "tired," she said.

That sentiment was echoed in online right-wing forums, said Jennifer Golbeck, a University of Maryland professor who has analyzed MAGA-related posts since 2016. She said engagement by Trump's most loyal backers has steadily declined since January, including a 27% drop in posts and comments on Patriots.Win, a popular MAGA forum.

"The enthusiasm and the passion even among this hardest core group of supporters hasn't really been there," Golbeck said. "They are saying that 'MAGA is stale.' It's not new and exciting like it once was."

Fox News, a cable network that has long been a key platform for MAGA voices, saw a sharp decline in viewership ahead of the midterms, with its total daytime audience down 27% in October from a year earlier, according to Nielsen, the audience measurement firm. In a statement to Reuters, Fox said it drew more viewers than its cable-news rivals on election night. "FOX News has been the number one network in cable news for a quarter century," spokesperson Caley Cronin said.

Some prominent right-wing influencers blamed the president's advisers or Republican lawmakers – but rarely Trump himself – for ignoring key voter concerns. In posts, online broadcasts and interviews with Reuters, many blamed dissatisfaction with the economy, though they differed on other reasons for Tuesday's results.

It wasn't just failure to address affordability that "crushed" Republicans, said Ben Shapiro, co-founder of the conservative site Daily Wire, on his online show on Wednesday. "If you're talking about an electoral catastrophe – ‌a wipeout like we saw last night – you need more ingredients. Here are the other ingredients: chaos and corruption."

Laura Loomer, an influencer close to Trump, wrote on X: "America is over and the American Dream is dead." Yet she told Reuters the losses did not signal the ​end of MAGA, arguing that anyone seeking the 2028 Republican presidential nomination would need Trump's base.

"The Republican Party belongs to President Trump," Loomer said. "The MAGA movement is still the majority of the GOP base, and whoever wants to run for president in 2028 on the GOP ticket, they would be ​unwise to be dismissive of President Trump."

On Thursday, Loomer put her podcast on hiatus, saying she had been "running on empty for too long" and needed to focus on her personal life and upcoming wedding. She'll return in January, she ​added.

The midterms also tested the beliefs that have held MAGA together, and some of them are giving way.

The Democratic sweep dealt a significant setback to the election denial movement, a central pillar of MAGA politics since Trump's 2020 defeat. Candidates who embraced his false claims of widespread voter fraud lost heavily, including several who had worked to overturn the 2020 result. Election deniers will hold ‌at least 41 fewer congressional and statewide offices next year, and they have lost 70% of the called races for statewide posts that oversee elections, according to States United ​Action, a nonprofit that tracks such candidates. Trump made no effort to contest the results and instead blamed Republicans for the defeat.

With ​few close races and no credible basis for a challenge, many prominent pro-Trump election skeptics dropped fraud allegations and urged supporters to keep organizing. A handful of allies still alleged, without evidence, that the vote was rigged. Mike Lindell, the MyPillow founder and promoter of false claims that machines flipped votes in 2020, said he was not concerned by Trump's pledge to accept the results. "That's his opinion. I've got a different opinion," Lindell told Reuters. "I think it's all been stolen."

But such claims stayed largely on the fringe, even among Republicans. Without contested races, the MAGA election denial movement risks losing the money, attention and momentum that sustained it. "Nobody's going to be putting money behind it," said Wendy Via, co-founder of the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism, a nonprofit that tracks hate speech and extremism.

Retired Lieutenant General Mike Flynn, who falsely claimed the 2020 election was stolen and is a popular figure ​in the Christian nationalist wing of the MAGA movement, accepted the defeat. He called the results "a massacre" and criticized Trump and his administration for failing to deliver on pledges ranging from ‌lowering costs to releasing the government's investigative files on Epstein.

Responding to Vice President JD Vance's assessment on X that the Iran war was "the reason we lost," Flynn wrote: "the sheer number of broken promises is why the blue tsunami happened."

Flynn also criticized Christian voters for failing to show up. "As a Catholic and a Christian, I'm sorely embarrassed and disappointed," he wrote.

Other prominent Christian nationalists were divided over whether MAGA can outlast ​Trump.

Douglas Wilson, a Christian nationalist pastor who was invited by US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to deliver a sermon at the Pentagon in February, told Reuters that MAGA "is not going anywhere" but must become less personality-driven and more focused on border control, tax cuts and avoiding foreign wars.

Joel Webbon, a far-right Christian nationalist pastor from Texas, was far less sanguine. "Trump lost this all by himself," he said in a ​video on X, arguing that the president abandoned his base by embracing Israel, launching the war in Iran and failing to follow through on releasing the Epstein files and mass deportations.

"MAGA is dead," Webbon wrote in an accompanying post. "Forever."

articles.body:
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) provided an update on the Last Frontier’s closely watched Senate race as vote counting continues.

“It’s very close,” the Alaska Republican said in an interview with John Catsimatidis on WABC radio, giving an update on what lies ahead in the process.

He said that there is a “big batch” of votes coming in next week on Nov. 13, followed by a “smaller batch” on Nov. 15. The final count will happen on Nov. 25.

The batch next week “will really determine who’s going to have the lead there because, right now … candidate Peltola is up by just I think a couple of hundred votes,” said Dunleavy, who was term-limited and could not seek reelection this year. The gubernatorial race to replace him remains uncalled.

“If nobody reaches 50 percent, that’s when they go through the ranking process in which the other candidates, the ones that have the least votes, they fall off and their votes are redistributed in the manner by which people rank them,” the governor added.

“We’re still in the process of bringing in votes and counting votes and we are in the midst of investigations to determine if there was any wrongdoing, especially anything that might resemble perjury or a misrepresentation of individuals’ intent on how they want their candidacy to be placed on the ballot,” Dunleavy said.

Alaska and Mississippi are the two states with remaining uncalled Senate contests.

The Senate race in Alaska between Democrat Mary Peltola and incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), was dragged into controversy in the weeks leading up to the midterm election.

The Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of the state’s election, claiming the presence of a candidate with the same name as the incumbent could give Peltola an unfair advantage. Days before the election, the New York Times reported that the Democrat’s campaign was directly involved in recruiting a man named Daniel J. Sullivan in an effort to dilute votes. Peltola has repeatedly denied the allegations.

Following the Times report, Dunleavy ordered an investigation into whether Peltola’s campaign violated state law, and the House Oversight Committee launched its own probe into the alleged scheme.

The race has been neck-and-neck with Peltola taking a slight lead over the incumbent with a little over 48 percent of the votes, according to Decision Desk HQ. Sullivan, on the other hand, has secured 47.9 percent of votes with 70 percent of the expected votes counted.

articles.title: MAGA voters reveal who they want to see lead GOP in 2028
articles.summary: MAGA voters at a Trump rally name JD Vance and Marco Rubio as early 2028 presidential election favorites after Democrats swept the midterms.
articles.body: With Democrats taking control of Congress in the midterm elections, MAGA voters are already sizing up potential successors to President Donald Trump in 2028 — with Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio repeatedly emerging as favorites among those interviewed by Fox News Digital. "I like [Rubio]," one American told Fox News Digital. "I like that he's no-nonsense, similar to Trump." "Well, I like JD Vance obviously," another said. "I like Marco Rubio. There's some other ones, too, that are maybe not so much mainstream that are coming up that I like too." TRUMP TOLD DONORS 'WE NEED TO ELECT JD,' SOURCE CONFIRMS, AS HE WEIGHS VANCE OR RUBIO IN 2028 "JD is great too, but Rubio has a little more experience," one said. "He's articulate, he’s well-spoken. He's got good ideas. I just really like him." Fox News Digital spoke with Americans attending a Trump rally in Bangor, Maine, as one of Trump’s final stops before Tuesday’s midterms that ended in a stunning blue wave. Fueled by anger over high costs and the war with Iran, Americans voted to oust Trump and his agenda, boosting Democrats to large majorities in the House and Senate. With Democrats looking to rebuke Trump and his allies, Republicans that Fox News Digital spoke with are looking for a presidential candidate to fill in Trump’s "footsteps." articles.title: Democrats won — now they must clean house
articles.summary: Democrats now have a golden opportunity to make good on their commitment to reform, but only if they learn from the past.
articles.body:
On Nov. 3, Democrats took control of Congress in large part by tying government corruption to the rising cost of living. As Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) put it, “Corruption is why things don’t work for the American people.”

Democrats should now deliver on the demand of 49 Democratic congressional candidates to make comprehensive anti-corruption legislation Congress’s “first order of business.”

In a 2027 version of the New Deal’s 100 Days, Congressional Democrats should make a downpayment on their promise to address affordability by raising the federal minimum wage; restoring cuts to child care tax credits, health insurance, Medicaid and SNAP; and rolling back tariffs. They should also investigate the Trump administration’s ethical abuses and put forward a series of concrete anti-corruption reforms.

Some of this legislation may die in the Senate or be blocked by a president who proclaimed he would be “ Mr. Veto ” if Democrats prevailed in the midterms. But some bills are likely to pass. And every rejection can become another plank in Democrats’ 2028 platform.

Eighty-nine percent of Americans believe corruption permeates the government .

Politicians often campaign on an anti-corruption platform, only to break their promises. Even Donald Trump, who has used the presidency to amass billions for himself, his family and his friends, pledged in each of his presidential bids to “ drain the swamp .” Asked recently about voters’ concerns, he insisted “there’s massive corruption ” among Democrats, but “we are straight and we are solid.”

Democrats now have a golden opportunity to make good on their commitment to reform, but only if they learn from the past.

After regaining control of the House in 2019, Democrats made the “ For the People Act ” a top priority. It combined ethics reform with provisions on voting rights, redistricting and campaign finance. The bill passed the House on a party-line vote but was attacked as a “ partisan power grab ” by Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), who refused to bring it to the Senate floor. By focusing their ire on the bill’s election provisions, Republicans did not have to justify opposing new ethics rules. A revised version died by filibuster in 2021.

By advancing a series of unbundled reform bills, Democrats can force Republicans to justify their objections, one vote at a time.

They should start by cleaning up their own House, literally. The Senate has already barred its members from betting on prediction markets . When Congress returns on Jan. 3, the newly Democratic House majority should ban members and staff from using inside information to make such bets.

Next, Congress should bar legislators, staff, senior executive branch officials and members of their immediate families from trading individual stocks. Trump endorsed a weaker version of this that would not apply to the president or vice president in his 2026 State of the Union address. Democrats should force him to sign a comprehensive bill or explain a veto.

Unlike most executive branch employees, the president and vice president are exempt from the principal criminal financial conflict-of-interest statute. Democrats should require them to divest assets that pose substantial conflicts or place them in blind trusts.

A separate bill should mandate disclosure when large donors or their businesses receive federal contracts or grants. Such legislation would give the public a chance to assess whether campaign contributions are influencing government decisions.

Absent a constitutional amendment, Congress cannot directly limit the president’s ability to use the pardon power to benefit political allies, donors and friends. But it can and should require disclosure of relevant financial relationships and Justice Department pardon recommendations.

Congress must also strengthen the referees.

The post-Watergate system relied on inspectors general to investigate agency misconduct , an Office of Government Ethics to handle executive branch conflicts of interest and an Office of Special Counsel to protect whistleblowers and enforce restrictions on partisan political activity.

Since returning to office, Trump has systematically dismantled these guardrails . In response, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer proposed a new Anti-Corruption Bureau with broad investigative and enforcement powers that would absorb the Federal Election Commission, Office of Government Ethics and Office of Special Counsel.

Since mixing election oversight with ethics enforcement might prove administratively cumbersome and invite constitutional challenges, we recommend strengthening existing institutions with ample funding, greater investigative authority and stronger protections against politically motivated interference.

We realize that cleaning up Washington will take more than one election, especially since the Supreme Court has given the president broad authority to fire agency heads and ethics enforcers. And Trump has demonstrated repeatedly his willingness to circumvent legal constraints .

The post-Watergate reforms established safeguards that constrained public officials for decades. Republicans may filibuster new safeguards or Trump may veto them. But Democrats should make them defend those choices, one bill at a time, and prepare to make them pay a price for self-dealing in 2028.

David Wippman is emeritus president of Hamilton College. Glenn C. Altschuler is the Thomas and Dorothy Litwin Emeritus Professor of American Studies at Cornell University.

articles.title: Democrats’ midterm sweep opens path to bypassing Electoral College by 2028
articles.summary: Democrat trifectas in key swing states could push the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact past 270 electoral votes needed to activate it and thus change...
articles.body:
Democrats' midterm gains have opened a new front in the fight over how America chooses its president — one that could reshape the 2028 race for the White House.

Democrats now control the governor's office and both chambers of the state legislature in Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada. The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, already enacted by 18 states and Washington, D.C., has 222 electoral votes pledged to it — 48 short of the 270 needed to take effect. If the four states join, their combined 50 electoral votes would push the compact to 272 and activate it. Arizona could push the total to 283 if Democrats ultimately gain control of both chambers there.

National Popular Vote (NPV), the nonprofit organization that authored the compact and is campaigning to enact it state by state, says it has identified multiple legislative sponsors in each of the five states whose combined electoral votes could push the compact over the 270-vote threshold. It expects bills to be pre-filed before, or introduced early, in the 2027 legislative sessions.

"I am confident we have multiple paths to secure the 48 electoral votes required to deliver what 63% of Americans want," Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant for NPV, told Fox News Digital.

Under the current electoral system, every state except Maine and Nebraska awards its electoral votes to the candidate who wins the statewide vote. If the compact takes effect, participating states would instead award their electors to the candidate who wins the most votes nationwide, leaving the Electoral College formally in place but making the national tally decisive.

Supporters argue the compact would give every vote equal weight by counting ballots toward a single national total. The Electoral College, by contrast, was structured to give both populous and smaller states a meaningful role in choosing the president.

"They can't use a compact to, in essence, change the Electoral College," Hans von Spakovsky, an election law expert with the conservative group Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital when asked about the potential activation of the compact before the 2028 election.

"This is unprecedented," von Spakovsky, a former commissioner on the Federal Election Commission (FEC), continued. "In the past, the only kind of compacts that have been agreed on between states have been things like water sharing — when rivers run between states, they enter into compacts to agree on that. But a compact that changes a fundamental structural given in the Constitution , I think the Supreme Court would say you can't do that."

Rosenstiel rejected the argument that the compact would improperly alter the Constitution, saying NPV believes Article II, Section 1 gives states the authority to determine how their presidential electors are appointed.

"Any clean read of Article II, Section 1 makes it clear that states have the exclusive power to award electors," Rosenstiel said. "The only credible legal question is whether this compact requires congressional consent."

Von Spakovsky argued that because the NPV compact is an agreement between states, Congress would have to approve it under the Constitution's compact clause in Article I. He noted Congress could approve the compact with simple majorities in the House and Senate and that the Constitution does not explicitly require the president's signature — meaning a presidential veto might not stop it.

However, von Spakovsky added that states choosing not to participate in the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would have a strong basis for litigation.

"Given that the NPV is entirely a creation of Democrats and only supported by Democrats, the new Congress will no doubt easily pass this compact," he told Fox News Digital. "However, I believe the non-participating states would have a good basis for litigation, which would end up in the Supreme Court, arguing that the compact is unconstitutional because it changes a fundamental structural part of the Constitution without going through the constitutional amendment process. The argument would be that states cannot make agreements among themselves that damage the federal system provided by the Constitution."

National Popular Vote's campaign has identified sponsors in all five potential additions following the midterms that could help push the compact over its 270-vote threshold and plans to begin pushing bills before or early in the 2027 legislative sessions, according to Rosenstiel.

Rosenstiel said the compact would apply to the 2028 election only if states representing at least 270 electoral votes join before July 20 of that year. That gives state lawmakers, Congress — if approval is required — and the courts less than two years to resolve the political and constitutional questions.

Until then, the Electoral College remains unchanged.

"I'm increasingly confident we can achieve that goal and we will have a national popular vote for president in 2028. I would certainly prepare for it," he said.

articles.title: Dana White says he will meet with Trump to discuss White House press secretary role
articles.summary: Dana White, president and CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), on Saturday said he will meet with President Trump on Monday to discuss the president’s offer to take the role of White House press secretary. White told reporters in London that he was flying to Washington and, when asked how he could balance multiple…
articles.body:
Dana White, president and CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), on Saturday said he will meet with President Trump on Monday to discuss the president’s offer to take the role of White House press secretary.

White told reporters in London that he was flying to Washington and, when asked how he could balance multiple jobs at once, said he has “a lot of jobs already.”

“We have a meeting on Monday, so I’m sure I’ll have more to talk about after that,” he said, not going into detail about his conversations with the president.

Earlier in the day, White shared what appeared to be an AI-generated image of himself standing behind the podium in the White House briefing room on his Instagram story. A caption read, “On to the next chapter.” He followed this with a screenshot of Trump’s Truth Social post saying he spoke with White about the role.

Trump on Saturday said that White was offered “the job of Press Secretary of the United States.”

“I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris,” Trump wrote. “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!”

Trump and White have had a close friendship in recent years. White’s UFC hosted a fight on the White House South Lawn over the summer as part of ongoing celebrations for America’s 250th anniversary and Trump’s 80th birthday. The CEO of UFC’s parent company, Andrew Schleimer, said it lost $30 million on the White House fight.

The White House has been searching for a permanent press secretary after Karoline Leavitt left in August.

Political commentator Katie Zacharia briefly held the role before she was dismissed after less than a week and only one short press briefing. Zacharia left the post after reports emerged that she had marketed herself as an attorney without passing the bar exam.

The search for a new press secretary also comes amid other shake-ups since Democrats made massive gains following the 2026 midterm elections. Former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles departed weeks after Trump wrote online that she was “my trusted advisor, and has my COMPLETE confidence.”

Stephen Miller, a long-time Trump adviser and formerly deputy chief of staff, replaced Wiles on Friday.

articles.body:
President Trump is set to appear on CBS News's "60 Minutes" Sunday night, sitting for his first interview following the GOP's devastating loss of both the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterms.

Post Election Day, the president was quick to blame Republican candidate quality for the sweeping blue wave, though others pointed to Trump's approval rating dip — brought on, in part, by his unpopular war in Iran, aggressive immigration policy and sweeping tariffs, among other key policy issues.

The Trump administration also has a rocky history with "60 Minutes" itself, as the show saw several prominent departures after CBS News's parent company, Paramount Skydance, was purchased last year by Larry and David Ellison — the father-son billionaire duo who are allies of the president. The media firm recently finalized a high-profile acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, which it bought out for $110.9 billion.

Meanwhile, members of Congress are preparing to return to Capitol Hill this week, some duking it out for leadership positions within their respective parties after Democrats flipped both chambers. Insiders can read more about the House and Senate have planned for the lame-duck period here .

articles.body:
Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) made an appearance on “Saturday Night Live” (SNL) over the weekend following his historic win in the Lone Star State in Tuesday’s elections.

The sketch — called the “ Post-Midterm Cold Open ” — featured two cast members dressed as Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), respectively played by Sarah Sherman and Kenan Thompson. The pair was celebrating the Democratic Party’s win in the election, which saw the caucus take definitive control of the House and Senate.

The Democrats were interrupted by President Trump, played by James Austin Johnson, who lamented the GOP’s losses this election cycle. Towards the end of his monologue, he referenced Trump’s nickname for the incoming Senator from Texas: “Talafreako.”

Talarico appeared from the wings and introduced himself as “the guy who’s been texting you every day asking for $5.”

“In this economy, who can blame you?” Trump’s parody said.

“But I think, Mr. President, if we can work together, we can make life better for everyday Americans,” Talarico told the audience. “It’s clear people want something new. They want something different. I’m talking, of course, about SNL’s cold opens.”

The sketch also included parodied cameos from Vice President Vance and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which mentioned attempts in the House to impeach the head of the Pentagon.

Though SNL is known for its comedy, Talarico has been honest while on the campaign trail about working with Trump and the MAGA movement on expanding health care access, building new homes and “slash[ing] the red tape.”

Talarico expressed in an interview with “ The Diary of a CEO ” that there was “still time to do that” in the last two years of Trump’s second term in the White House “on a bipartisan basis.”

“So my hope is that this midterm will be a wake-up call for the president, for his administration, and as a result, they will reverse course,” he concluded.

As of Sunday, Talarico is ahead of Paxton by around 12 points with over 95 percent of the ballots counted in a surprise win for Democrats in the red stronghold, according to The Hill’s partner, Decision Desk HQ .
