articles.title: Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton says he’d be disappointed if Democrats focus on investigating Trump
articles.summary: Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said that he hopes to prioritize lowering costs and that he would be “deeply disappointed” to spend two years investigating Trump.
articles.body: Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, who flipped deep-red Kansas for Democrats, said Sunday that he hopes to prioritize lowering costs for his constituents in the next Congress and that he would be “deeply disappointed” to spend two years investigating members of the Trump administration. “The bigger priority for me, and I think for most people in America, especially people living paycheck to paycheck, is ‘please help us with the cost of living,’” Hamilton told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” Specifically, he said the new Congress should immediately focus on ending the war in Iran and “claw[ing] back tariffs policies.” “If I spent the next two years — my first two years in the Senate — in investigations, I’d be deeply disappointed. I want to get to work helping the people in my state and helping the people across the country,” Hamilton said. After Democrats’ landslide victories Tuesday, which granted them control of the House and Senate in the next Congress, newly elected leaders and those who were re-elected are turning to focus on their priorities for the next two years. Many are calling on colleagues to focus on an affordability agenda, but some senior leaders have said that they’ll also prioritize oversight and investigations into possible corruption by President Donald Trump and his allies. “Whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court and entangle him in legislative razor wire,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters Wednesday. Several Democrats, including Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who served as an impeachment manager for one of Trump’s impeachments during his first term, have floated potentially impeaching the president for a third time. “I’m not as interested in impeachment as setting up guardrails,” Hamilton said Sunday, though he added, “I understand the move and the desire to do this.” Instead, the senator-elect said his party should concentrate on making life more affordable for Americans. “Let’s focus on helping the American people,” he said. “And I’ll tell you, the Democrats, if they don’t, if we don’t figure that out and get to work on helping people, this is going to be a one and done, kind of, you know, kind of blue wave.” Appearing later on the program, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., agreed with Hamilton. “I think the senator-elect Hamilton made a good point,” Sanders told “Meet the Press,” adding: “We cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump. We have to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives.” With Democrats winning in 54 Senate seats and two more Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled, Schumer could be poised to take over as Senate majority leader in the next Congress if a majority of the Democratic members of the Senate vote in his favor. Hamilton has said that he doesn’t plan to support Schumer’s bid to be majority leader. On Sunday, he said he has “no disrespect for Chuck Schumer,” but “I just really don’t [want him as majority leader], and I’ve told him that as well.” The senator-elect cited the volume of TV ads during the campaign linking him to Schumer, which he said addressed the fact that “a lot of people in Kansas feel, who may not know Chuck Schumer personally, who don’t know him personally, but you know that that they perceive him to be further to the left, and somebody who’s a divisive figure.” He demurred when asked who he might support over Schumer, saying, “I know probably 10 senators personally, and even those I only know from brief conversations. So, you know, I’m not at a place where I can tell you, ‘these are, this is my short list.’” Hamilton added: “There are a handful of people that I think are probably, you know, lead more from the center, but I don’t know enough yet to be able to say, ‘these are the people I would endorse.’”

articles.title: Three ways the new Congress can stop Trump’s war
articles.summary: Following Democratic victories in the midterm elections driven by opposition to the Iran war, the incoming Congress plans to utilize its power of the purse, potential impeachment proceedings against the Defense secretary, and litigation to force the Trump administration to end the conflict.
articles.body:
The “Blue Wave” that swept Democrats to victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections was powered by public opposition to President Trump’s disastrous war of choice with Iran. In exit polls, 74 percent of voters said the Iran war was a crucial or major factor in their vote.

Seven in 10 voters want Congress to prioritize ending that war , which it never authorized.

Even with healthy majorities in both chambers, making good on that mandate won’t be easy. After all, a congressional majority has already voted to stop this war: in June, both houses directed the president to withdraw U.S. troops from hostilities, yet here we are.

Even so, the incoming Congress has several constitutional tools to push Trump toward ending the war. Let me name just three.

First, Congress can refuse to fund the war. The most effective leverage Congress has capitalizes on what it usually does best: nothing. It doesn’t take a supermajority to defund a war; all it takes is for one chamber of Congress to refuse to pay.

The Trump administration has spent nearly $50 billion on “Operation Epic Fury” so far, even though Congress has yet to pass specific appropriations for it. But in a conflict this expensive, creative accounting only goes so far. Facing “an urgent budget shortfall” this summer, the administration requested Iran war funds; that request now sits with the Senate, which can tighten the squeeze just by letting it sit.

The power of the purse has historically been Congress’s “most effective way” to force presidents to change course, the Congressional Research Service notes . But maximizing that leverage requires more than simply standing pat.

During the Nixon administration, a resurgent Congress used appropriations riders to help wind down the Vietnam War, imposing a hard cutoff on combat operations in Southeast Asia after Aug. 15, 1973. Twenty years later, after Black Hawk Down, similar tactics helped end our nation-building excursion in Somalia.

The 120th Congress can follow the same playbook: conditioning funding on withdrawal by a date certain.

Second, Congress can impeach Trump’s Defense secretary, reinvigorating a constitutional weapon dulled by the Trump era. In mid-September, Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) rushed the House to early recess to avoid a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The articles, drawn up by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), are coming right back: the Republican gadfly intends to force a vote this week when the House returns.

Four of the eight articles in Massie’s bill of particulars center on Iran: that he is carrying out an illegal war in violation of the Constitution’s Declare War clause and multiple provisions of the 1973 War Powers Resolution.

Amid a deeply unpopular war, constitutional censure by the House could really leave a mark. True, Trump could moot the effort by firing Hegseth. But either way, the goal shouldn’t be simply getting a scalp, but imposing costs for continuing an unnecessary, unconstitutional war.

Third, the new majority can bring in the courts. The first branch can enlist the help of the third, the federal judiciary.

In July, after Trump blew past the War Powers Resolution’s time limits and the resolution directing him to withdraw, Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) moved to enforce the law in court. Under Meeks’s bill, the House would sue the president, with Johnson dragooned into the role of lead plaintiff (no doubt apologizing to Trump the whole way).

Article III courts are ordinarily loath to intervene in war powers fights between the political branches. Past attempts by House members to sue presidents over unauthorized warmaking have been bounced for lack of standing .

But when the House as an institution files suit, the case has a much better shot at getting heard. In 2020, when the House sued Trump for illegally diverting funds to his border-wall project, the D.C. Circuit granted standing because Trump’s gambit had effectively “snatched the House’s key out of its hands.”

Johnson may be able to put off the suit, but in January, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) gets the Speaker’s gavel and the House can take Trump to court.

Would a federal court declare the war illegal? That’s unlikely. But, win or lose, both Meeks’s lawsuit and Massie’s impeachment drive will keep the war and the constitutional arguments against it in the front of the public mind.

Survey experiments by political scientist Douglas L. Kriner indicate that congressional opposition to war framed in constitutional terms is especially persuasive because “most Americans, like the Framers, still desire collective judgment in questions of war and peace.”

Meanwhile, Congress can keep the pressure on by wielding its most powerful weapon: the power of the purse.

Congress doesn’t need new powers or bigger majorities to fulfill its constitutional responsibilities and bring an end to an illegal war, it needs to start using the powers it has.

Gene Healy is a senior scholar at the Reason Foundation and author of “The Cult of the Presidency .”

articles.body: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he hopes Democrats prioritize healthcare and food assistance when they take control of Congress in January, though he urged them not to forget to hold the Trump administration accountable. “I hope one of the first things that the Congress does is to stop these Medicaid cuts, stop the SNAP cuts, roll back the cuts, the effective cuts in the Affordable Care Act,” Shapiro said in an interview with NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that aired Sunday. Shapiro noted that in Pennsylvania alone, 510,000 people are losing healthcare and 143,000 more are losing SNAP or food assistance due to cuts approved during President Donald Trump’s second term. “In general, though, I think Democrats need to have an aggressive agenda that cuts costs, that ends the war, that gets put on the president’s desk,” he said. “Hopefully, he will sign it because it’ll be common-sense stuff that makes people’s lives better.” Trump has said that he intends to work with Democrats when Congress begins its new term, though he has also touted a new “VETO”-branded hat since Republicans lost the majority in the midterm elections. Shapiro said that if Trump chooses to veto Democrats’ legislation, “it’s yet another signal to the American people the president actually doesn’t care about their well-being.” While the governor stressed the importance of revitalizing Medicaid and SNAP programs, he also said Democrats shouldn’t forget to hold the Trump administration accountable. “I think the Congress needs to be responsive to where voters are on corruption, and there has to be real accountability for this administration,” Shapiro said, adding that Democrats need to “walk and chew gum at the same time” to pass effective legislation and also “have real accountability for the corruption that exists in Washington.” “It can’t be either/or,” he said. “It has to be both/and.” Shapiro added that Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to become the next speaker of the House, “has made very clear that both are going to be on the agenda for the first 100 days and for these next two years.” The governor said that he doesn’t think Democrats should be thinking about the 2028 elections yet. Instead, “we should be thinking about how to make people’s lives better in 2027,” he said. “It’s incumbent upon the Congress to now do that, and it’s incumbent upon governors now to continue to lead the way in our states,” Shapiro said. Shapiro, who has been floated as a potential 2028 presidential contender, did not commit to running. Asked whether he is more likely to run than not, Shapiro answered that his focus was on “figuring how we advance policies like raising the minimum wage and many other things that have been blocked by Republicans,” as Pennsylvania Democrats won a majority in the state legislature Tuesday. He also did not directly answer whether he was committed to serving his full four-year term. “Well, I committed to run for governor, and that’s the work I’m focused on doing,” Shapiro said. “And if I’ve got something to say about my future, I’d love to come back on your show and talk about it.”

The phrase "finish the job" has become synonymous with toppling the 47-year ironclad totalitarian rule of the Islamic Republic. IRAN’S REGIME WON’T NEGOTIATE IN GOOD FAITH. Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile remains unaccounted for under international verification, and the regime has retained the ability to rebuild elements of its ballistic missile program. Former Pentagon official Simone Ledeen told the London-based Iran International news organization the Islamic Republic "needs to end" and regime will never change its behavior. TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME Veteran Iran observers and experts have noted that President Trump was the first U.S. leader not to kick the Iran nuclear weapons problem down the road. AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR? The U.S. should continue to maintain its blockade of Iran and facilitate shipping from the Persian Gulf, but except hitting well-protected and highly dangerous targets, such as nuclear sites if needed, the US should stay out of continuous attacks because its internal political situation is messed up." articles.title: Jon Meacham on the midterms and America's "better angels"
articles.summary: In last week's historic elections, voters were asked to weigh in on whether our nation will maintain the ideals of equality, dignity, fair play, and the rule...
articles.body:
What does Tuesday's seismic election say about America today? Perspective from Pulitzer Prize-winning author and historian Jon Meacham:

In his long retirement in Independence, Missouri, Harry Truman spent a great deal of time musing about democracy and history. "The country," he remarked, "has to awaken every now and then to the fact that the people are responsible for the government they get."

This week an American electorate woke with a start, registering a protest of historic dimensions. From Maine to Kansas , the Democratic Party upended years of assumptions about what was thought to be the most static of political landscapes, producing victories that reminded everyone — Democrat, Republican, and Independent — of the raw and resonant power of the ballot.

Democracy is messy because we (you and I) are messy. The American Founders understood this. "If men were angels," James Madison wrote, "no government would be necessary"— and given that men are so self-evidently un-angelic, the American government was designed to check our passions and balance our failings.

For a decade now, the issues of our own un-angelic moments have been profound: Is the United States a sustainable enterprise grounded in equality, dignity, fair play, and the rule of law? Are we a republic that respects elections that go the other way? Are we a country with politicians and partisans able to lose graciously, and win graciously?

These questions transcend red and blue; they're bigger than any policy debate or tax rate. And for the moment, the people have answered them affirmatively and definitively. The verdict has been accepted. The people have been heard. Democracy has prevailed.

The Greeks were right: character is destiny — and destiny in Greek can also be translated as "fate." And so, America's fate depends on our dispositions of heart and of mind, on our capacity not to fear but to hope, on our willingness to heed not our worst instincts, but the better angels of our nature.

This much is clear: Those better angels had a good week, because democracy had a good week. No matter your party, that's good for America, and Americans.

Story produced by Robert Marston. Editor: Jason Schmidt.

articles.title: Blanche dodges questions on investigating Democrats
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche dodged questions on Sunday on whether he would open investigations into Democratic members of Congress following President Trump’s remarks to look into claims of a “criminal act.” Appearing on CNN’s “State of the Union,” Blanche was asked about Trump ordering investigations against Congressional Democrats for calling for the impeachment of certain…
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche dodged questions on Sunday on whether he would open investigations into Democratic members of Congress following President Trump’s remarks to look into claims of a “criminal act.”

Appearing on CNN’s “State of the Union,” Blanche was asked about Trump ordering investigations against Congressional Democrats for calling for the impeachment of certain cabinet officials.

“Well, what we‘ve seen over the past several days and even over the past several weeks are outright threats,” the attorney general said. “They‘ve threatened donors. They’ve threatened individuals who are in college and might want to work for conservative institutions or for a conservative government or for President Trump. And that is extremely troubling.”

“They’re already talking about investigations and impeachments with no basis, no facts, just out there running around. That should be something that President Trump is very concerned about and certainly I am as well,” Blanche continued.

Host Dana Bash responded, stating Democrats were “talking about investigation as part of their oversight role. That is prescribed by the constitution.”

“They have a very unique role in oversight, I agree,” Blanche said. “Have you been listening to the rhetoric the past couple of days?”

The attorney general expressed he had heard talks of impeachment and going after private companies who made government investments, remarking this was “not oversight.”

“So are you saying that you are going to investigate them? And what you just described is there a crime there,” Bash asked.

“It depends on what‘s said,” he said. “So yes…you have free speech in this country. You are allowed to be critical of President Trump, of me, of this administration. But when the threats become so vile and so dangerous that you are telling people in college that they better be careful if they want to work in the Trump administration, because somebody will come after them at some point. You have to draw the line.”

Blanche’s leadership at the DOJ has faced renewed scrutiny following Tuesday’s elections, including for the department’s intervention in Alaska’s Senate election and defense of White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.

Reps. Hank Johnson (D-Ga.) and Deborah Ross (D-N.C.) have already floated the idea of impeaching Blanche following Democrats regained control of the House and Senate.

articles.title: Trump says U.S. took a "giant step back in history" with midterm results
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday said the U.S. "took a giant step back in history" as his White House continued to roil from his post-midterm shakeup
articles.body:
Latest updates on 2026 midterm election results:

President Trump on Sunday said the U.S. "took a giant step back in history" as his White House continued to roil from his post-midterm shakeup , including his announcement that Stephen Miller will replace chief of staff, Susie Wiles. Mr. Trump gave his first sit-down interview since the midterm elections with "60 Minutes'" Ross Douthat, which will air Sunday at 7 p.m. ET/PT on CBS and Paramount+ . And sign up for the 60 Minutes newsletter to make sure you never miss a minute.More results continued to trickle in this weekend, with Democrats celebrating having flipped more than 40 Republican districts — some of which were viewed as deep red — and staving off major losses from redistricting . Democrats will hold at least 54 Senate seats and around 256 seats in the House in January, CBS News estimates.More than 20 House races and two Senate contests remain unresolved . In Mississippi's Senate race, Democrat Scott Colom leads by about 2,500 votes as ballots continue to be counted. If he ultimately prevails, it would be one of the biggest political upsets in recent memory.Find updates on key House races here , and all election results in the CBS News Election Center .

Adam Hamilton says if Democrats don't "get to work on helping people," blue wave will be "one and done"

Adam Hamilton, who last week became the first Democrat elected to the Senate in nearly a century, said if he spent his first two years in Congress on investigating the Trump administration, he would be "deeply disappointed."

"I want to get to work helping the people in my state and helping the people across the country. So what I'm interested in is: Yes, let's get guardrails put in place so that we don't see these kind of things happen again. But let's focus on helping the American people," Hamilton said on NBC's "Meet the Press."

Hamilton, a centrist who defeated GOP Sen. Roger Marshall after launching what once seemed a long-shot bid in Kansas, said there should be focus on corruption in Washington. But he said if Democrats don't "get to work on helping people, this is going to be a one-and-done kind of blue wave."

"Our campaign was built around trying to bring people together," Hamilton said. "I don't want to see us spend the next two years dividing our country further, I want to see us come together to look at solving really big problems."

Shapiro says he believes there will be a "robust primary challenge" against Fetterman in 2028

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who was reelected by over 20 points on Tuesday and helped carry the Democrats to a trifecta in the state's government, told "Meet the Press" on Saturday that he believes there will be a "robust primary challenge" to Democratic Sen. John Fetterman.

"I think that there's no question that people are lining up to run, and he has to decide if he's going to run," Shapiro said.

Shapiro, who is considered a 2028 presidential contender, said he had spoken to Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina after the midterms, but wouldn't comment on the "private conversation" they had.

When asked if his decision to run would be influenced by whether or not former Vice President Kamala Harris runs for president, Shapiro said: "I think everyone should make their decisions on their timelines in the way that they see fit."

Hakeem Jeffries says he hasn't spoken to Trump since midterm victories for Democrats

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, whose party made massive gains in the midterm elections that could result in his election as House Speaker in the new year, said he has yet to speak to President Trump, as the leaders prepare for divided government in Washington.

"We'll see what happens in terms of moving forward. But I have spoken to three former presidents, and I'm thankful for those conversations," Jeffries said on ABC's "This Week."

Jeffries, a New York Democrat, said, "most importantly," he's had to chance to speak to everyday Americans who "were the ones that powered this election and want us to actually deliver a Congress that no longer functions like a reckless rubber stamp for Donald Trump's extreme agenda, but functions like a separate and co-equal branch of government designed to make life better for the American people."

Asked whether he will be able to work with the president, Jeffries said, "The country clearly has had enough, and we've got to fight for an affordable America." He pointed to Democratic priorities including ending the war in Iran and the president's tariffs, along with reversing Medicaid restrictions.

"We'll see whether our colleagues on the other side of the aisle actually are willing to listen to the American people, so we can work to get things done," Jeffries said, adding that the sizable Democratic majorities in the House and Senate will allow the party to "get to work."

Trump says U.S. "took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election"

As President Trump headed to play golf on Sunday, he posted on social media that the U.S. "took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election."

"Even the Stock Market, which has been a 'ROCKETSHIP' under 'TRUMP,' took a one day, 3 Trillion Dollar loss. But have no fear, we will be back, BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!" Mr. Trump's post continued.

The stock market had a roller-coaster week last week, buoyed Wednesday by the election results and then tanking Thursday amid a steep tech selloff . The stock market bounced back on Friday.

James Talarico makes appearance on "Saturday Night Live"

Texas Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico appeared on "Saturday Night Live" for the cold open on Saturday, telling cast member James Austin Johnson that "it's clear that people want something new, they want something different."

Talarico introduced himself to cheers, saying he is "the guy who's been texting you every day, asking for $5."

"I think Mr. President, if we can work together, we can make life better for everyday Americans. It's clear that people want something new; they want something different," he said, before adding, "I'm talking of course about SNL's cold opens."

Talarico joined Johnson to chant "Live from New York, it's Saturday night!"

Peltola files lawsuit against Alaska DOE over rejected absentee ballots

Alaska's Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola filed a lawsuit on Friday against the state's Department of Elections seeking to review rejected absentee ballots.

"We are confident that Mary will win this race," the Peltola campaign said in a statement. "The campaign is ensuring transparency, timeliness, and accuracy as the counting process continues and every Alaskan's voice is heard."

The Alaska Beacon first reported on this suit.

Peltola currently holds a slim lead over incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, although the state uses ranked-choice voting and tabulation will take place on Nov. 18. Ahead of that deadline, the Department of Elections is still waiting to count tens of thousands of absentee ballots, some of which have not yet been received.

The race's certification is scheduled for Nov. 25.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen urges colleagues to avoid rushing to select their next Senate majority leader

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland urged his Democratic colleagues to show restraint in the selection process of their Senate majority leader in the wake of the party's dominant showing in the midterm elections this week.

"There should be no coronation," Van Hollen said during an interview Saturday at the Crooked Con political conference in Washington, D.C. "I said very clearly that we need to have a discussion in the Democratic Caucus. We need to understand what the Democrats are going to do with this new responsibility and these new powers, and that nobody should get a blank check without a full understanding from the caucus as to where we're going to go."

The Democrats will hold at least 54 seats in the upper chamber when the new session of Congress convenes in January. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has led the Senate Democratic Caucus since 2017, but several incoming Democratic Senators-elect have signaled they want to see new leadership.

"This is why I said it's really important that people withhold any commitments on the Senate leadership races until we have a chance to hear from our new members who just got off the campaign trail and have been directly in touch with voters," Van Hollen said.

On Friday, a Van Hollen aide told CBS News the Maryland senator will not pursue the majority leadership post.

Sen. Mark Kelly says he is considering 2028 presidential bid

Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona disclosed Saturday he is considering a 2028 presidential run.

"I am thinking about it," Kelly said when asked in an interview at Crooked Con, a political conference held in Washington, D.C., hosted by the media group Crooked Media.

The 62-year-old Kelly, a former NASA astronaut and Navy combat pilot, was among those being considered as the running mate of then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 when she replaced former President Joe Biden as the Democratic presidential nominee.

"We've had conversations," Kelly added. "We're going to continue to have."

Trump claims Alaska Senate race "is over" but counting is still underway

President Trump weighed in on the Alaska Senate race on Saturday, claiming that the incumbent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, has won, even though counting is still underway.

"Daniel Sullivan is leading substantially in the Alaska Senatorial Race. When you add Daniel (3,600, 1.68%) into Dan, and Gerald Heikes (4,846, 2.27%), Senator Dan Sullivan is up by thousands of Votes," Mr. Trump said in a Truth Social post. "I don't know what takes so long to announce his win."

The contest that has garnered widespread attention over the two candidates named Dan Sullivan faces a lengthy ballot-counting process. Alaska has a ranked-choice voting system , which allows voters to rank as many or as few candidates as they'd like in order of preference.

Approximately 74% of the votes have been counted as of Saturday, according to The Associated Press.

Democrat Mary Peltola is leading Sen. Sullivan by over 600 votes, which is shy of the 50% of votes required to win.

If nobody wins an outright majority once all the votes are counted, the count goes to a second round. The candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated, and their supporters' votes are redistributed to their second choice. That process continues until one candidate wins a majority.

"This should be immediate! Anyone voting for Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr., a man who tried to change his middle initial, but was unable to get it done in time, and who was otherwise nonpolitical – Never even voted – is a vote for Senator Dan Sullivan," Mr. Trump said Saturday. "The Alaska Race is OVER. Dan Sullivan WON, BY A LOT!"

Talarico visits memorial of Houston man killed by ICE in first public appearance since election night

Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico visited the memorial of a father who was shot and killed in July by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer in Houston on Saturday.

Talarico joined hundreds of others in placing his "I voted" sticker at the memorial of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, his campaign said in a statement. The visit is Talarico's first public appearance since election night, when he defeated Republican Ken Paxton and flipped the seat for Democrats for the first time since 1988 .

"Lorenzo Salgado lived in this country for 35 years. As a construction worker, he sent his three boys to college. Lorenzo Salgado embodied the American dream. He was a child of God, endowed with infinite worth. Lorenzo, our fellow Texan, deserves justice — and that's exactly what I'll fight for in the U.S. Senate," Talarico said in a statement.

The visit also marks four months since Salgado Araujo was killed in Magnolia Park, a neighborhood that has been a hub for the Mexican American community for a century.

Trump to order DOJ to investigate impeachment threats

President Trump said Saturday that he is ordering the Department of Justice to "look into" what he describes as threats by Democrats to impeach senior Republican figures, calling them "extortion at the highest level."

In a Truth Social post, Mr. Trump said Democrats are "threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General of the United States, and others" with impeachment and "many other forms of punishment, even though they admit they have no reason to do so."

"There have been no impeachable acts committed, or even thought of, by the victims of this illegal process," he said. "This is extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable for this."

Mr. Trump accused Democrats of also threatening GOP donors with imprisonment and other punishments "just because they happen to be Republicans, or Republican supporters."

"This is Weaponization and Lawfare at another level," he wrote, adding that it was the Democrats who should be facing "imprisonment" and calling them "EXTORTIONISTS", writing in his trademark capital letters.

The president's post comes just days after Democrats laid out plans to investigate Mr. Trump and others in the administration.

They said the subjects they would focus on would include the Trump family's business dealings, corporate corruption, actions of the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who will chair the House Oversight Committee next Congress, singled out Stephen Miller, Corey Lewandowski, Kristi Noem and Trump family members as particular individuals they would target. Miller was named Mr. Trump's chief of staff on Friday.

Republican Rep. Mike Kennedy wins reelection in Utah's 4th District

Republican Rep. Mike Kennedy has won reelection in Utah's 4th Congressional District, CBS News projected.

Kennedy, who previously served in the Utah state Senate and House, beat out challenges from Democrat Jonny Larsen, Independent Steven Burt and Libertarian Taylor Wright.

"Thank you, Utah! I'm humbled by your trust and grateful for the opportunity to continue serving you in Congress," Kennedy wrote in an Instagram post after his win.

Rep. Aisha Wahab wins full term in California's 14th District

Democrat Rep. Aisha Wahab wins reelection to the U.S. House in California's 14th district, CBS News projected.

Wahab beat fellow Democrat Melissa Hernandez in a rematch of August's special election to fill the seat vacated by former Rep. Eric Swalwell.

The embattled lawmaker resigned in April amid sexual misconduct allegations, which he has denied.

Wahab, the first Afghan American elected to Congress, previously served in the California state Senate.

Trump told 60 Minutes he was planning some post-midterm firings. Hours later, he announced Susie Wiles' departure.

President Trump announced that Stephen Miller would replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff just hours after he told 60 Minutes that he'd be shaking up his team.

When 60 Minutes Correspondent Ross Douthat asked Mr. Trump whether he expected to fire anyone after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress, the president said: "I do, yeah. Little bit."

"I love my Cabinet. I think they're good," he said. "But I'll … be doing maybe a few changes."

Trump says "the Senate has to act" before new Congress takes office

Asked about his priorities for the lame-duck session before Democrats take control of the House and Senate, President Trump told reporters : "The Senate has to act."

"The Senate is getting nothing passed, and it's just killing our country," he said, calling the upper chamber a "roadblock" and "one of the problems we had" in the midterms. He later pointed to the SAVE America Act, a package of voting restrictions that Mr. Trump pressed Senate Republicans to take up for months, though Senate Majority Leader John Thune said it couldn't pass.

"We had a bad election because of a few things. One thing was not getting things approved in the Senate," he later said.

Mr. Trump called Thune a "good man," but said he's "got to get things done." Asked if Thune is the right person to serve as Senate GOP leader, he said: "It's going to be up to the Republicans. They choose, I don't choose."

Democrats flip outgoing GOP Rep. Nancy Mace's South Carolina district

Previewing the party's plans starting next year, the minority leader said: "Whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court, and entangle him in legislative razor wire."

Many congressional Democrats are likely to be enthusiastic about investigating the Trump administration. But one moderate incoming Democratic senator, Adam Hamilton of Kansas, told CBS News he wants to spend more time on cost-of-living and other issues than investigations or impeachments, saying: "I do not want to spend the next two years in trials."

Asked about the potential for Democrat-led investigations, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said: "As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

Talarico says his Texas Senate win sends message to Elon Musk: "Texas is not for sale"

Democrat James Talarico on Wednesday said his win over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race delivered a message to Elon Musk, who spent more than $150 million to boost Paxton's candidacy: "Texas is not for sale."

Hours after his projected win over Paxton, Talarico told "CBS Mornings" that his victory is an opportunity to get big money out of politics "for good."

"The people of Texas delivered a crystal-clear message to the world's first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale," Talarico said. "The power in this state, in this country, belongs to the people and we've got to make sure it stays that way."

articles.title: North Carolina rep requests ‘nonpartisan election observers’ in close race
articles.summary: Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.) is requesting “nonpartisan election observers” in her House race as she trails behind Democratic opponent Chuck Hubbard. “Election integrity is not a mere suggestion – it is the keystone of free and fair elections that have always guided the course of our nation throughout history,” she wrote in a Facebook post.…
articles.body:
Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.) is requesting “nonpartisan election observers” in her House race as she trails behind Democratic opponent Chuck Hubbard.

“Election integrity is not a mere suggestion – it is the keystone of free and fair elections that have always guided the course of our nation throughout history,” she wrote in a Facebook post . “The counting process for the 5th District election has not halted. The count is ongoing in accordance with North Carolina state law.”

Foxx described how the “continuing process, our laws and faithful election administration” would determine her race “and nothing else.”

“At my request, nonpartisan election observers under the guidance of the Committee on House Administration will be present across the 5th District as the count continues, and will serve as important, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,” the lawmaker continued.

Foxx continued that the observers were dispatched under the “Confirmation of Congressional Observer Access Act.”

The act allows for states to provide “congressional election observers” to watch the “administration procedures of federal elections.” It explicitly prohibits observers from handling ballots or election equipment, campaigning for a particular candidate or interfering with the elections administration process.

“My work in service to the constituents of the 5th District remains ongoing, and my offices continue to stand at the ready to assist. The process will continue,” Foxx concluded in her post.

The lawmaker is currently trailing behind Hubbard, according to the reported totals from the Associated Press as of Sunday morning. The outlet estimated 99 percent of the ballots had been counted, showing the Democrat currently leading by 99 voters, making this race one of the closest margins this election cycle.

She is among the dozens of House Republicans projected to be swept away in the midterm’s “blue wave.”

In North Carolina, the GOP already lost five seats with only one seat left open, including the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.), being defeated by Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.)

articles.title: How sports apps hooked a generation of women
articles.summary: If current trends hold, women could be gambling as much as men. But equal opportunity to lose is not progress.
articles.body:
In September, actress Sydney Sweeney appeared, covered by little more than footballs and other sports gear, in a national ad for the betting platform Novig. Olympic swimmer Ariarne Titmus called it “a kick in the face to every woman who had dedicated her life to perfecting her craft.”

Then, in October, Sweeney and Novig answered with a sequel , topless again, under the same slogan: “Just sports.” It drew a fresh round of complaints . “Why do you have to be naked to market sports?” one commenter asked.

Both rounds of outrage were about what the ads said about women athletes. But the women with the most reason to be offended went unmentioned: the silent, growing number of female gamblers.

Betting ads should be restricted the way tobacco ads are, and betting apps should be made to tell users the truth about what they are losing and what their real odds are.

Sports betting is usually described as a man’s habit. But since the Supreme Court opened the door to legal sports betting nationwide in 2018, betting has exploded; last year, Americans wagered $166.9 billion . Women made up 35 percent of online sports bettors last year, up from 26 percent in 2022, according to the American Gaming Association.

In ads like Sweeney’s, a woman’s body is the draw. In others, featuring Kendall Jenner or Lisa Leslie , women are the customers. So are women the bait or the bettor?

This fall, the Wheatley Institute surveyed a nationally representative sample of 2,665 American adults about their gambling habits and beliefs. What surprised us was how many young women are now placing bets. Forty percent of women under 30 reported betting on sports through an app at least once a year, compared with 24 percent of women overall, and nearly a third reported using a prediction market at least once a year.

These women are not simply dabbling. Elaina Bozzuto, a 30-year-old Connecticut mother, lost as much as $200,000 on a betting app over three years before filing for bankruptcy, Bloomberg Law reported. One in five women in our survey said that in the past year she had gone back another day to win back money she had lost. About one in six had lied about her gambling, and about one in eight had needed someone to bail her out. Of those who had deleted a betting app, roughly two-thirds later downloaded it again.

They also bet from a weaker position. Only about half of the women we surveyed described their finances as good or excellent, compared with 69 percent of men. That is a costly place to start in a game where 96 percent of online gamblers appeared to lose money over five years, according to a UC San Diego study of more than 700,000 Americans.

For half a century, we have measured women’s progress in part by how closely their lives converge with men’s. Now they are converging in vices, too. The gap between men’s and women’s drinking, once more than two to one, has nearly closed among younger people. Gambling appears to be following the same path.

As scholars who study human flourishing , we look at close relationships, financial security, mental health and character. Gambling works against each of them . It is a business that does well only when nearly everyone who plays it does not .

Many young adults sense this. Half of adults under 30 said betting is morally wrong and can lead to addiction, more than any other age group. Yet 60 percent had had a betting app on their phones. Across all ages, people who called gambling morally wrong still gambled about as often as everyone else.

It is not that young people lack a conscience about gambling. It is that their conscience doesn’t win out.

Adults under 30 told us they learned about gambling from YouTube (42 percent) and TikTok (27 percent) far more often than from their own families (17 percent). A public education campaign should meet them there and explain why betting is no reliable way to earn money. Betting apps should carry clear warnings about addiction and a number to call for help, and prompt users to set a spending limit before their first deposit, as Britain already requires .

Lawmakers should restrict betting ads as they restricted tobacco ads. The 1998 settlement banned billboards, cartoons and youth targeting. A 2025 review linked tobacco advertising bans to a 37 percent lower risk of starting smoking. Keep betting ads away from young audiences and off live sports broadcasts. We should watch games without being sold a gambling habit.

The debate over Sweeney’s ads asked whether they were fair to women athletes. It might have asked about the women being sold the bet.

If current trends hold, women could soon be gambling as much as men. But equal opportunity to lose is not progress.

Shima Baradaran Baughman is the Woodruff J. Deem Professor of Law at Brigham Young University’s J. Reuben Clark Law School and a distinguished fellow at the Wheatley Institute. Stephen Cranney is a data scientist with a Ph.D. in demography and sociology from the University of Pennsylvania and an appointment at the Catholic University of America.

articles.title: 11th-hour power play targets incoming Dem governor after historic GOP defeat
articles.summary: Republican Texas Rep. Brian Harrison urged Greg Abbott to convene a special session restricting emergency powers before Gina Hinojosa is sworn in.
articles.body: A GOP lawmaker in Texas is seeking to limit some of the incoming governor's powers after Democrats flipped the state blue in Tuesday's election. Republican Texas state Rep. Brian Harrison on Wednesday publicly urged outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott to convene a special session to "rein in" the governor's executive emergency powers before Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa takes office. "Republicans lost last night, but Democrats were not sworn in," Harrison wrote in a lengthy statement posted on X. "We still have total power in Texas, and we must act like it by using the remaining ten weeks to restore separation of powers and limit the emergency powers that Governor-Elect Hinojosa is set to inherit, that would allow her to destroy liberty in Texas by executive fiat." Harrison also emphasized in the post that he believes Texas governors should not have "unchecked" emergency powers, regardless of their party affiliation. TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES "Texas should have reined in executive emergency powers when I first demanded it in 2022," Harrison told Fox News Digital on Thursday. "If these are not revoked, Gina Hinojosa will assume not just the powers our state constitution bestows upon a Governor, but will, in effect, inherit nearly all the powers of a dictator. Most people are shocked to learn Texas governors can write, edit, or change any statute on a whim if they just declare an ‘emergency,’ and this is unconstitutional." Under Section 433.002 of the Texas Government Code, the governor may issue emergency directives and "amend, modify, or rescind" those directives during a declared state of emergency, subject to the requirements outlined in the law. "These powers have been abused in the past, and Governor-Elect Hinojosa has pledged to use them on day one," the Texas Republican added. "Republicans are still in control for ten weeks, we need to start acting like it." Harrison also said in the X post that the Texas Legislature should "immediately pass" legislation such as HB911, which he filed in December 2022 to restrict the governor’s "never ending emergency powers." His comments come after Hinojosa defeated Abbott in Texas' 2026 gubernatorial race on Tuesday, becoming the state's first-ever Latina governor. While on the campaign trail, Hinojosa pledged that she would declare "a high-cost emergency" in Texas and introduce executive orders to halt the state's gas and diesel taxes and to freeze residential electricity rates, the Texas Tribune reported Wednesday. Abbott's office and Hinojosa's campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. In a Thursday X post, Harrison claimed that his demand to curb the Texas governor's emergency powers "has REALLY triggered low-IQ leftists across America," adding that he did not "recall them cussing and calling me every name in the book when I filed the same legislation 4 years ago... right after ABBOTT was re-elected!!" The governor of Texas possesses the ability to sign or veto bills passed by the state's Legislature, serve as commander-in-chief of the state's military forces and convene special legislative sessions "for specific purposes," according to Abbott's office. Under the Texas Disaster Act of 1975, the governor can declare a state of disaster and exercise certain emergency powers, including suspending specific regulatory requirements, but disaster declarations must be renewed after 30 days and can be terminated by the Legislature at any time. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI Hinojosa vowed in a Wednesday X post that her administration will "lead with a politics of courage, not convenience." The Democratic Party notched another key victory in the Lone Star State on Tuesday after James Talarico toppled Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the U.S. Senate race. Ahead of Hinojosa taking office next year, some Republican Texas state senators have pledged to "hold the line" against Democrat-led policy goals in the state, The Houston Chronicle reported Wednesday. President Donald Trump on Tuesday blasted Abbott in a Truth Social post, claiming the governor lost his re-election bid because he is a "RINO," an acronym that stands for "Republican in name only." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn’t become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost," Trump wrote in the social media post. "He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!" After conceding the race, Abbott told supporters on Tuesday that he had informed Hinojosa that he "would assist her and her team in a period of transition," The Hill reported. "For weeks, I had been publicly warning on this podcast that we were in very real danger of losing everything in Texas," Republican Texas Sen. Ted Cruz said Wednesday in an X post. "Far too few believed that was possible. I am very, very sorry that it came to pass. Texas has not had a Democrat governor since 1994." "We haven’t had a Democrat senator since 1993," Cruz added. "Now we’ll have both." Hinojosa is set to officially take office in January 2027.

articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries says he’s a ‘hard yes’ to impeach Hegseth
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who will likely be the Speaker of the House come January, said Sunday that he is a “hard yes” when it comes to impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. “I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution. The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security…
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who will likely be the Speaker of the House come January, said Sunday that he is a “hard yes” when it comes to impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution. The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran,” Jeffries said to ABC News’s Jonathan Karl on “This Week.”

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) had told Karl that he intends to introduce a resolution of impeachment against the defense secretary.

On Thursday, Hegseth shot back against threats of impeachment in a video posted to the social platform X. He said in the video that “a disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly,” referencing Massie.

“Just like they tried against President Trump twice. You see, their policies don’t work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It’s all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that,” Hegseth added in the video.

Jeffries’s comments also come after Democrats won both the House and the Senate in this year’s midterm elections earlier this week, most likely stymieing the Trump administration’s agenda for the next two years.

The House minority leader’s comments also followed him posting Thursday on the social platform X, “Why is Pete Hegseth still around?”

The Hill has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday morning shared a “Family Guy” style cartoon of Dana White as the White House press secretary after the president on Saturday said he offered White the role.

The UFC CEO responded to the president and reporters in London Saturday night, saying that he will meet with Trump on Monday to discuss.

The president is also set to appear on CBS News’s “60 Minutes” Sunday night, sitting for his first interview following the GOP’s devastating loss of both the House and Senate in Tuesday’s midterms.

Post Election Day, the president was quick to blame Republican candidate quality for the sweeping blue wave, though others pointed to Trump’s approval rating dip — brought on, in part, by his unpopular war in Iran, aggressive immigration policy and sweeping tariffs, among other key policy issues.

The Trump administration also has a rocky history with “60 Minutes” itself, as the show saw several prominent departures after CBS News’s parent company, Paramount Skydance, was purchased last year by Larry and David Ellison — the father-son billionaire duo who are allies of the president. The media firm recently finalized a high-profile acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, which it bought out for $110.9 billion.

Meanwhile, members of Congress are preparing to return to Capitol Hill this week, some duking it out for leadership positions within their respective parties after Democrats flipped both chambers. Insiders can read more about the House and Senate have planned for the lame-duck period here .
